subject: Model selection affects adjusted ungulate counts

messages.author: fed273b6d100226b
messages.subject: Model selection affects adjusted ungulate counts
parts:
Hi all,

 

Hoping you can help me answer some questions related to issues that I am having understanding the results of my analyses.

 

Quick outline of my study design and what I plan to analyze:

I am studying three target ungulate species: bighorn sheep, elk, and mule deer. I have stratified my study area into “open” areas and “forested” areas, as detection of ungulates will most certainly differ in each of these habitats. Thus, I wish to model each of these 6 datasets (3 species x 2 habitats) with a separate detection function then calculate the probability of detection for each dataset. Distances were calculated from observer to group centroid exactly (distances were not binned in the field). I am using CDS as a way to adjust summed ungulate counts within sampling units across my study area. Each sampling unit has a mean distance from unit to survey transect. I will later model each species’ habitat use using adjusted species counts and environmental covariates as predictor variables.

 

Here is the general approach that I have followed for each dataset (separately):

-Fit a simple preliminary model (half-normal key + cosine adjustment) to explore the non-truncated datasets

-Examined histograms for failure to meet distance sampling assumptions (ie: heaping at 0 distances, movement prior to detection, rounding distances etc.)

-Determined truncation distances based on g(w) = 0.15

-Fit same 6 potential models to 6 datasets

-Examined AIC, chi-sq GOF, and K-S GOF results

-Selected top model then calculate probability of detection and adjusted counts within sampling units


I have attached a spreadsheet (Model_Comparisons).

 

Questions:

Q1:

From everything I have scoured within this forum, and from the Buckland et al. (2001) book, I understand that I should select the top model based on AIC, while also ensuring that my data meet GOF tests. For example, in my open bighorn analysis, the top model based on AIC was the uniform key function with a cosine adjustment term (with 3 orders). The GOF chi-sq p-value 0.490 > 0.05 and the GOF K-S p-value 0.79 > 0.05. The QQ plot showed that the model fit the data well, as did the histogram (screenshots attached). This is how I selected the top models for each of my 6 datasets (selected top models are highlighted in attached spreadsheet). When competing top models were within 2 AIC values (and each model adequately met GOF tests and QQ plots & histograms showed good model fit), I rationalized that this meant each model could adequately represent my data and, thus, it didn’t really matter which model I selected. So, I still went with the lowest AIC value to retain consistency in my approach. I also understand that when there are competing top models, I could model average or I could consider the model that is most parsimonious, as AIC tends to select for models with more parameters (or less-parsimonious models). I do not wish to model-average as I would argue that any of my top models should be adequately able to adjust my ungulate counts sufficiently. Does this approach make sense? Am I missing something?

Q2:

When I went to actually calculate the probability of detection for each species x habitat type, I ran into some issues. Take ‘open elk’ for example. I’ve included my R script used to calculate probability of detection, as well as the top model output for ‘open elk’ from Distance 7.1, below. The top model, based on my approach listed in Q1, is the half-normal key function with no adjustment terms. When I calculated the probability of detection based on y distances, the probabilities ranged from 0 to 0.99. The adjusted counts, therefore, ranged from 2.42 x E39 groups per sampling unit to 0 groups per sampling unit. Obviously, something is wrong because there is no way that there are 2.42 E39 elk groups in a small sampling unit. After experiencing this issue, I decided to adjust counts based on the other competing top model from ‘open elk’ to see if I could get better estimates and to cross-reference. This was the uni+cos model (model output and R script below). I’ve also attached a spreadsheet that compares the probabilities of detections and adjusted counts for each competing top model for open elk (the spreadsheet is a subset of my data). Basically, what I have found is that I was not at all correct with assuming that just because both of these models came out as “competing top models” that they could equally represent my data. So, why are my adjusted counts so biologically illogical? Does this mean that I should not be selecting my top models in the manner I described in Q1? Why are the adjusted counts for the half-normal so different from the adjusted counts from the uniform+cosine, when both models are within 0.64 AIC values and meet the model fit standards that I described in Q1? Are the adjusted counts poor because I am extrapolating detection functions determined from right-truncated data (400 m for open elk dataset) to distances > 400 m? Should I remove data > 400 m from my habitat use analysis, since I cannot accurately predict detection of ungulate groups past this distance? This would certainly limit the application of my results as I would have a much smaller effective study area. Are my data not meeting some assumptions that I somehow missed in my data examination? How should I proceed to accurately adjust my counts for detectability while ensuring they are biologically relevant?


Thanks in advance,


Meghan Beale

University of Alberta

Department of Biological Sciences

parts:
Meghan

This was a lot to take on board on a Friday afternoon.  My boss usually saves emails with 9 attachments for special occasions.

I'll give you some partial answers.  I'm comfortable with what you describe as your "general approach" and the model selection you did as seen in your spreadsheet and Question 1 all make sense.

I didn't make my way through your Q2 and associated R code because I got stuck on whether you were trying to produce design-based estimates of abundance (with the conventional distance sampling engine) or model-based estimates; the final sentence of your outline suggests the latter.  What has me stuck are these "sampling units".  I don't really know what these are, nor how they relate to the distance sampling survey you conducted.

The simplistic answer to the beginning of your Q2 "calculate the probability of detection for each species x habitat type" would be to take the value of "P" as produced by Distance 7.1 (0.527 for your open-elk half-normal model and 0.519 for open elk with uniform-cosine model).  As you said, those are species and habitat-specific estimates of detection probability because you stratified your data prior to analysis.

Your adjusted count spreadsheet eludes me.  Perhaps we'll continue this discussion offline and you can help me understand what you're hoping to accomplish, then provide a summary to the list.
